etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English savegard, from Middle French sauvegarde, from Old French salve garde, sauve garde, reconstructed as safe +‎ guard.

definitions.definition: Something that serves as a guard or protection; a defense.

quote.citation: 1983, D. C. Pandey, Habitual Offenders and the Law, page 31:
quote.text: An externment of a person is a harsh punishment on him and calls for procedural safeguards against the abuse of power by the authorities.

definitions.definition: One who, or that which, defends or protects; defence; protection.

quote.citation: 1726, George Granville, To the King, in the First Year of His Majesty’s Reign:
quote.text: Thy sword, the safeguard of thy brother's throne.

definitions.definition: A safe-conduct or passport, especially in time of war.

quote.citation: c. 1608–1609 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Coriolanus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: the inheritance of their loves and safeguard
The same idea is entertained of the Safeguard in America, as of the Monitor in Africa, and other parts of the Old World,  […]

quote.citation: 2020 November 18, “Network News: London 'bailout' achieved with just minutes to spare”, in Rail, page 10:
quote.text: "[...] Crossrail 2 is mothballed. It is safeguarded, it is absolutely not cancelled."

definitions.definition: (UK, Ireland, by extension) To implement safeguarding.
